context.heading: A historian's word for certainty
context.body: Luke writes so that Theophilus may know the asphaleia ("certainty, security") of what he has been taught. The word describes something made firm or fastened; Acts 5:23 uses it of a prison locked "securely." Luke opens his Gospel with a researcher's preface, not a vision, because the faith rests on events that can be traced and tested.

context.heading: Chosen by lot for one hour
context.body: Zechariah served in the division of Abijah, one of twenty-four priestly rotations (1 Chronicles 24:10). With so many priests, the honor of burning incense in the holy place was assigned by lot (lanchanō). Later Jewish tradition suggests a priest might do it only once in his life. God meets Zechariah on the biggest day of his career, in the middle of an ordinary duty roster.

context.heading: Overshadowed like the tabernacle
context.body: Gabriel says the power of the Most High will episkiazō ("overshadow") Mary. The Greek Old Testament uses this word for the cloud that settled on the tabernacle when God's glory filled it (Exodus 40:35), and Luke uses it again for the cloud at the Transfiguration (9:34). The conception of Jesus is God's own creative presence at work, not a human union.

theology.title: The God who remembers
theology.body: Zechariah's name means "the LORD remembers," and both songs in this chapter say God has remembered His covenant and His oath to Abraham (vv. 54–55, 72–73). Barren Elizabeth stands in the line of Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, and Gabriel's "nothing will be impossible with God" (v. 37) echoes the word to Sarah (Genesis 18:14). John comes in the spirit of Elijah, picking up exactly where Malachi ended (Malachi 4:5–6).

theology.title: David's Son and God's Son
theology.body: Gabriel's promise of a throne, a house and a kingdom without end repeats God's covenant with David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Yet this child is also called holy, the Son of God, because He is conceived by the Holy Spirit (v. 35). The church confesses this in the Apostles' Creed: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary. The long-promised King is God the Son taking on real human flesh.

application.title: Questions versus conditions
application.body: Zechariah and Mary both question Gabriel, but Zechariah wants proof before he will believe, while Mary believes and asks how it will happen. God welcomes honest questions, but He is not obligated to meet our terms.
application.question: When you question God, are you looking for understanding or setting conditions for your obedience?

application.title: Faithful through the quiet decades
application.body: Zechariah and Elizabeth walked blamelessly for years while carrying the public shame of childlessness (v. 25). God's answer came during a routine shift at work, long after they had stopped expecting it.
application.question: What unseen faithfulness are you tempted to quit because nothing seems to be happening?

application.title: A yes that costs a reputation
application.body: Mary's "let it be to me" (v. 38) meant being an engaged young woman who was visibly pregnant in a small town. Her obedience came before anyone understood her.
application.question: What would saying yes to God cost you in other people's eyes this month?

context.heading: A full guest room, not a rude innkeeper
context.body: The word usually translated "inn" is katalyma, the same word Luke uses for the upper guest room of the Last Supper (22:11); for an actual inn he uses a different word (10:34). Many scholars think Joseph's family stayed with relatives whose guest room was already full. Village homes often kept animals in the lower room at night, which would explain the manger.

context.heading: The offering of a poor family
context.body: Forty days after a birth, a mother brought a lamb and a bird for her purification. The law allowed two doves or pigeons for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:6–8). Mary and Joseph bring the poor family's offering. The Son of God grew up in a household that counted every coin.

context.heading: A sword through Mary's soul
context.body: Simeon warns Mary that a rhomphaia, a large broad sword, will pierce her own soul. Her son will be "a sign that will be opposed," exposing the hearts of many. The warning reaches its fulfillment at the cross, where Mary stands watching her son die (John 19:25).

theology.title: Comfort for Israel, light for the nations
theology.body: Simeon waits for the "consolation of Israel" and Anna for the "redemption of Jerusalem" (vv. 25, 38), language from Isaiah's promises of comfort (Isaiah 40:1; 52:9). Simeon's song adds that this salvation is a light for the Gentiles (Isaiah 49:6). God keeps His word to Israel and, through Israel's Messiah, opens His blessing to every nation, as He promised Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

theology.title: Fully God, truly growing
theology.body: At twelve, Jesus speaks of the temple as "My Father's house" and says He "must" be there (v. 49), showing He knows His unique relationship with God. Yet He goes home and submits to His parents, growing in wisdom, stature and favor (vv. 51–52). Scripture holds both together: the eternal Son really lived an ordinary human childhood.

application.title: Good news for the night shift
application.body: God sends the first birth announcement to shepherds working through the night, not to priests or officials. Heaven's choice of audience still surprises us.
application.question: Who in your workplace or neighborhood do you quietly assume is least likely to care about Jesus?

application.title: Waiting without going sour
application.body: Simeon and Anna spent long years waiting, and Anna had been a widow for decades, yet both were alert and hopeful when the moment came. Long waiting made them sharper, not bitter.
application.question: What are you doing with the waiting season you are in right now?

application.title: Assuming He is in the caravan
application.body: Mary and Joseph traveled a full day assuming Jesus was somewhere in the group (v. 44). It took three days to find Him.
application.question: Where have you assumed Jesus is with you without actually checking?

context.heading: The word skips the palace
context.body: Luke lists an emperor, a governor, three tetrarchs and two high priests, then says the rhēma ("word") of God came to John in the wilderness. The phrasing echoes how the prophets' books begin (Jeremiah 1:1–2). Annas had been deposed by Rome around AD 15 but still held great influence while his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office (John 18:13).

context.heading: Snakes fleeing a field fire
context.body: John calls the crowds a "brood of vipers" (echidna) fleeing the coming wrath. The picture is of snakes racing out of a burning field of stubble. They want escape from judgment without the change of heart that repentance requires, so John's next image is an axe already at the root (v. 9).

context.heading: Shakedowns and false charges
context.body: John tells soldiers not to diaseiō, literally "shake violently," a slang term for extorting money by intimidation, nor to accuse people falsely for profit. These were probably Jewish troops serving Herod Antipas or guarding tax collection rather than Roman legionaries. John does not tell them to quit, but to stop abusing their power and be content with their pay.

theology.title: Father, Son and Spirit at the Jordan
theology.body: At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends and the Father speaks (vv. 21–22). "You are My beloved Son" echoes the royal Psalm 2:7, and "in You I am well pleased" echoes the servant of Isaiah 42:1. In the Greek Old Testament "beloved son" also describes Isaac (Genesis 22:2). From the start, Jesus is the King, the suffering Servant and the beloved Son offered by the Father.

theology.title: The LORD comes down the road
theology.body: John quotes Isaiah 40:3–5 about preparing a highway for the LORD Himself to return to His people. John prepares the way for Jesus, so Jesus is the LORD arriving in person. Luke alone continues the quotation to "all flesh shall see the salvation of God" (v. 6). God's coming is not only for one nation but for all humanity, which Luke underlines by tracing Jesus back to Adam.

application.title: Repentance with a job description
application.body: When crowds ask "What should we do?", John gives specific answers by occupation: share, charge only what is fair, stop bullying. Repentance shows up on the invoice and the timesheet.
application.question: If you asked John what repentance looks like in your actual job, what would he name?

application.title: The second coat
application.body: John tells anyone with two tunics to give one away (v. 11). He chooses something ordinary and specific, not something heroic.
application.question: What do you have two of, or more than enough of, that someone near you lacks?

application.title: Heritage is not a hiding place
application.body: The crowds lean on "We have Abraham as our father" (v. 8). John says God can raise up children from stones; family background cannot replace a changed life.
application.question: What are you relying on, such as upbringing, church history or reputation, instead of fresh obedience?

context.heading: Tested where Israel failed
context.body: Peirazō means both to test and to tempt. Forty days in the wilderness echoes Israel's forty years, and Jesus answers each temptation from Deuteronomy 6–8 (8:3; 6:13; 6:16), where Moses reviewed Israel's failures in the desert. Where Israel grumbled for bread and tested God, the Son trusts His Father completely.

context.heading: Gone until a better moment
context.body: The devil leaves Jesus "until an opportune time" (kairos). The word means a fitting or decisive moment, not just a span of time. Luke shows Satan returning when he enters Judas before the Passover (22:3). The wilderness victory is real, but the battle continues to the cross.

context.heading: Luke's favorite word: today
context.body: After reading Isaiah 61, Jesus says, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled." Sēmeron ("today") marks salvation arriving in Luke: a Savior is born today (2:11), salvation came today (19:9), today you will be with Me (23:43). Jesus stops reading before Isaiah's next line, "the day of vengeance of our God," which many see as deliberate: this is the season of favor.

theology.title: The obedient Son
theology.body: Luke's genealogy ends with "Adam, the son of God," and the devil immediately says, "If You are the Son of God." Adam fell in a garden; Jesus stands firm in a desert. He proves His sonship by trusting His Father's word, not by grabbing power. He is the faithful Son that both Adam and Israel failed to be.

theology.title: Grace that crosses borders
theology.body: Jesus reminds Nazareth that God sent Elijah to a widow in Sidon and healed Naaman the Syrian while many in Israel went without (1 Kings 17:8–16; 2 Kings 5). God's mercy has always reached outsiders. The crowd's rage shows how offensive grace becomes when it is not reserved for people like us. Even the demons recognize Him as "the Holy One of God" (v. 34).

application.title: Scripture as a reflex
application.body: Jesus answered temptation with verses He knew well enough to use while hungry and alone. He did not argue with the devil on the devil's terms.
application.question: Which specific verse would actually come to mind the next time you are tired and tempted to cut a corner?

application.title: Too familiar to hear
application.body: "Isn't this Joseph's son?" (v. 22). Nazareth could not accept a claim from someone they had watched grow up.
application.question: Where has growing up around church made you deaf to what Jesus actually claims?

application.title: Saying no to good demands
application.body: The crowds tried to keep Jesus from leaving, but He said He must preach in other towns too (vv. 42–43). He started His day alone before the requests came.
application.question: What good demand on your time is crowding out the thing God has actually given you to do?

context.heading: Master, at Your word
context.body: Peter calls Jesus epistatēs, "master" or "boss," a word only Luke uses in the New Testament, and only from disciples addressing Jesus. A professional fisherman defers to a teacher about fishing. After the catch he falls down and calls Him kyrios, "Lord" (v. 8). His view of Jesus grows in a single morning.

context.heading: Catching people alive
context.body: Jesus says Peter will be zōgreō, "catching alive." The word was used of taking prisoners alive in war instead of killing them. Fish caught in a net die; the people Peter will now gather are rescued for life.

context.heading: A touch before the cure
context.body: Skin diseases called leprosy made a person ritually unclean and forced to live apart and cry out "Unclean!" (Leviticus 13:45–46). Jesus touches (haptō) the man before he is clean, which would normally defile the one who touched. Instead, cleanness flows the other way. Jesus then sends him to the priest, as Moses commanded (Leviticus 14), to be restored to community.

theology.title: Who can forgive sins but God?
theology.body: The scribes reason correctly that only God can forgive sins (v. 21). Jesus does not correct their theology; He claims that authority as "the Son of Man," the heavenly figure who receives an everlasting kingdom in Daniel 7:13–14. He heals the paralyzed man so that a visible miracle will confirm an invisible authority.

theology.title: The bridegroom has arrived
theology.body: When asked why His disciples do not fast, Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom (vv. 34–35). The prophets pictured the LORD as Israel's husband (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus casts Himself in God's role and announces a time of celebration, while hinting that He will be "taken away." New wine needs new wineskins.

application.title: Obedience before results
application.body: Peter had worked all night and caught nothing, and his experience told him daytime fishing was pointless. He let down the nets anyway, because Jesus said so.
application.question: What instruction from Jesus are you delaying because your experience says it will not work?

application.title: Friends who dig through roofs
application.body: Four friends carried a paralyzed man and removed roof tiles to get him to Jesus (v. 19). Jesus saw their faith.
application.question: Who near you needs you to go to inconvenient lengths to bring them near Jesus?

application.title: Throw the party
application.body: Levi's first act as a disciple is a big banquet for his tax-collector friends (v. 29). He did not cut off his old network; he brought it to Jesus.
application.question: Who from your old circles have you never once invited into the life you now have?

context.heading: Harvesting by hand on the Sabbath
context.body: Plucking grain from a neighbor's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25). But the disciples also psōchō, "rub," the heads in their hands, and some Pharisees treated this as threshing, one of the kinds of work banned on the Sabbath. Jesus answers with David eating the consecrated bread (1 Samuel 21:1–6) and claims to be Lord of the Sabbath.

context.heading: Stamped paid in full
context.body: "Woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort." Apechō was a business term written on receipts, meaning "paid in full." Those who live for present comfort have collected their whole account; nothing more is owed to them.

context.heading: Lending with nothing expected back
context.body: In a world built on patronage, a gift or loan created an obligation to repay or honor the giver. Jesus says to lend apelpizō, "expecting nothing in return." The word normally means to give up hope of something. Disciples are to give in a way that puts no one in their debt.

theology.title: Like Father, like children
theology.body: Jesus grounds love for enemies in God's own character: He is kind to the ungrateful and the evil (v. 35). This is the God of Exodus 34:6, compassionate and gracious, who sends rain on people who never thank Him. Children of the Most High are recognized by the family resemblance.

theology.title: Twelve for a renewed Israel
theology.body: Jesus prays all night and then chooses twelve apostles (vv. 12–13). The number deliberately recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is gathering and renewing God's people around Himself, which is why His teaching that follows reads like a new covenant charter for the community.

application.title: A plan for your enemy
application.body: Jesus does not stop at "don't retaliate"; He says do good, bless and pray for those who hate and mistreat you (vv. 27–28). Love here is a set of actions, not a feeling.
application.question: What specific good could you do this week for the person who has most wronged or irritated you?

application.title: The log you carry
application.body: Jesus pictures someone with a beam in his own eye offering to remove a speck from his brother's (vv. 41–42). The faults we spot fastest are often our own.
application.question: What criticism do you most often make of others that is just as true of you?

application.title: Digging to bedrock
application.body: The wise builder digs deep before the flood comes (v. 48). Both houses look the same until the storm hits.
application.question: Which teaching of Jesus do you know well but have never actually put into practice?

context.heading: A Gentile who keeps his distance
context.body: The centurion was probably an officer in Herod Antipas's forces rather than a Roman legion. He knows a Jewish teacher would risk ritual impurity by entering a Gentile home, so he sends elders and then friends. His message, "I am not hikanos ("worthy, sufficient") to have You under my roof," is striking because the elders had just called him worthy (v. 4).

context.heading: Feet within reach
context.body: At formal dinners guests reclined on couches, leaning on one elbow with their feet stretched away from the table. That is how the woman could stand behind Jesus at His feet. Uninvited people could often watch such meals. Her alabastron ("alabaster jar") held costly perfume, and letting down her hair in public was considered shameful.

context.heading: Two debts cancelled as a gift
context.body: One debtor owed five hundred denarii, well over a year's wages for a laborer, and the other fifty. The lender charizomai, "freely forgave," both debts. The verb comes from charis, "grace": cancellation as a gift, not a negotiated discount.

theology.title: The Lord of life at Nain
theology.body: Jesus raises a widow's only son and "gave him to his mother" (v. 15), the same words used when Elijah raised a widow's son (1 Kings 17:23). Elijah prayed and stretched himself over the boy three times; Jesus simply speaks. The crowd says, "God has visited His people" (v. 16), and Luke wants readers to see that more is true than they know.

theology.title: Signs of the promised age
theology.body: To John's question, Jesus points to His works: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, the poor hear good news (v. 22). These are the signs Isaiah tied to God's coming salvation (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1). Jesus fulfills the promises even when His way of doing it surprises the faithful, and He blesses those who are not offended by Him.

application.title: Authority you already understand
application.body: The centurion knew how orders work: a word from someone with authority gets things done. He trusted Jesus' word without needing Jesus present.
application.question: In what area of your life do you treat Jesus' word as advice rather than as a command?

application.title: Doubt from a prison cell
application.body: John, the greatest of the prophets, sent his doubts straight to Jesus instead of nursing them alone. Jesus answered with evidence, not a rebuke.
application.question: When God does not act the way you expected, do you take your doubts to Jesus or away from Him?

application.title: The courtesies Simon skipped
application.body: Simon offered no water, no kiss and no oil; the woman gave tears, kisses and perfume. Jesus says the difference is how much each thought they had been forgiven.
application.question: What does the way you treat Jesus reveal about how much you think you have been forgiven?

context.heading: A secret meant to be told
context.body: Jesus says the disciples have been given to know the mystērion ("mystery") of the kingdom. In the New Testament a mystery is not a riddle but something once hidden that God now reveals. Quoting Isaiah 6:9, Jesus says the parables open truth to those who come close and hide it from those who keep their distance.

context.heading: A name like an army
context.body: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers, and Roman troops were a familiar, hated sight. The man lived among tombs in Gentile territory where pigs were raised, a scene saturated with uncleanness for a Jewish reader. "Legion" (legeōn) suggests both overwhelming numbers and occupying force. Jesus frees him with a word.

context.heading: Saved, not only cured
context.body: Twelve years of bleeding made the woman ritually unclean and largely excluded from worship and normal contact (Leviticus 15:25–27). Jesus tells her, "Your faith has sōzō you," a word meaning both "healed" and "saved." He calls her "daughter" and makes her restoration public, not just her cure.

theology.title: The one the sea obeys
theology.body: In the Old Testament only God rules the raging sea: He stills its waves and brings sailors to safe harbor (Psalm 89:9; 107:28–30). When Jesus rebukes the wind and water, the disciples ask, "Who then is this?" (v. 25). The Psalms already supplied the answer.

theology.title: Holiness that flows outward
theology.body: Under the law, touching a bleeding woman or a corpse made a person unclean. Jesus is touched by one and takes the hand of the other (vv. 44, 54). Instead of impurity flowing into Him, power flows out of Him (v. 46). God's holiness in Jesus is not fragile; it moves toward the unclean in mercy and makes them whole.

application.title: Thorns that look respectable
application.body: The seed among thorns is choked by worries, riches and pleasures (v. 14), none of them scandalous. Ordinary concerns can crowd out God's word as surely as open rebellion.
application.question: Which ordinary worry or comfort is quietly choking what God has planted in you?

application.title: Sent home, not on tour
application.body: The freed man begs to travel with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home to tell what God has done (v. 39). His first mission field was the town that had chained him.
application.question: Who at home most needs to hear what God has actually done for you?

application.title: The interruption on the way
application.body: Jairus's daughter was dying, yet Jesus stopped to find the woman who touched Him. He was not rushed by urgency into ignoring a person.
application.question: How do you treat the people who interrupt your urgent plans?

context.heading: A cross every day
context.body: Only Luke records "take up his cross daily" (kath' hēmeran). Everyone knew a man carrying a crossbeam was on a one-way walk to his execution. Luke turns that final act into a daily pattern: dying to self is not a one-time decision but a habit.

context.heading: Three tents on the mountain
context.body: Peter offers to build three skēnē ("tents" or "shelters"). He may be thinking of the Feast of Tabernacles or of the tabernacle where God dwelt with Israel. He wants to hold onto the moment, but the cloud and voice redirect him from building to listening.

context.heading: The Chosen One to listen to
context.body: The Father calls Jesus "My Son, the eklegomai ("Chosen One")," echoing God's chosen servant in Isaiah 42:1. "Listen to Him" echoes Moses' promise of a prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15). With Moses and Elijah standing by, the Father points past the Law and the Prophets to their fulfillment.

theology.title: Bread in a desolate place
theology.body: Jesus feeds five thousand in a remote place (v. 12), recalling God feeding Israel with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16) and Elisha feeding a hundred with leftovers to spare (2 Kings 4:42–44). Twelve baskets remain, one for each tribe or apostle. The God who fed His people in the desert is present and providing in Jesus.

theology.title: A Messiah defined by the cross
theology.body: Peter rightly confesses Jesus as "the Christ of God" (v. 20), and Jesus immediately says the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and be raised (v. 22). Popular hopes pictured a conquering king. Jesus fills the title with Isaiah's suffering servant (Isaiah 53). Even on the mountain of glory, the topic is His coming death.

application.title: The "first let me" problem
application.body: Three would-be followers each have a reasonable condition: a home, a funeral, a goodbye. Jesus says no one who keeps looking back is fit for the kingdom.
application.question: What "first let me" are you putting in front of following Jesus right now?

application.title: Welcoming those who add nothing
application.body: While the disciples argue about greatness, Jesus places a child beside Him and says welcoming such a one welcomes Him. A child offered no status or connections.
application.question: Whose company would cost you status rather than add to it, and how do you treat them?

application.title: Calling down fire
application.body: When a Samaritan village refuses Jesus, James and John want to call down fire on it (v. 54). Jesus rebukes them and simply goes to another village.
application.question: When people reject you or your faith, what do you secretly wish would happen to them?

context.heading: Seventy, or seventy-two
context.body: Ancient manuscripts differ between seventy (hebdomēkonta) and seventy-two sent out. Either way the number likely echoes the list of the nations in Genesis 10, which has seventy names in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. The mission hints at the gospel reaching every nation (Acts 1:8).

context.heading: A road with a reputation
context.body: The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops about 3,300 feet over roughly seventeen miles of rocky desert and was notorious for robbers. The Samaritan takes the man to a pandocheion, a public inn, pays two denarii, about two days' wages, and leaves an open account. Mercy here costs time, money and personal risk.

context.heading: Dragged in every direction
context.body: Martha is perispaō, literally "pulled around," distracted by much serving. Serving guests was an honorable duty, so the problem is not the work but being pulled away from Jesus' word. Mary sits at His feet, the posture of a disciple learning from a rabbi (Acts 22:3), a place usually given to men.

theology.title: The Son who reveals the Father
theology.body: Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and praises the Father (v. 21), a rare glimpse of the Trinity in joyful relationship. He says no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son reveals Him (v. 22). Knowing God is not achieved by cleverness; it is a gift the Son gives to the humble.

theology.title: The law's two great commands
theology.body: The lawyer sums up the law with Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18: love God completely and love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus agrees and says, "Do this and you will live." The parable then shows how far that love must reach, exposing how short everyone falls. Many readers, from the early church on, have also seen Jesus Himself in the Samaritan who rescues at His own cost.

application.title: Too busy to stop
application.body: The priest and Levite probably had reasons to pass by, perhaps schedules or fear of impurity. The Samaritan had reasons too, and stopped anyway.
application.question: Whose need have you passed by recently because stopping would have wrecked your schedule?

application.title: Rejoice in the right thing
application.body: The seventy-two return thrilled that demons obeyed them. Jesus redirects their joy to the fact that their names are written in heaven (v. 20).
application.question: If your visible results at work or church vanished tomorrow, what would your joy rest on?

application.title: Good work, wrong moment
application.body: Martha was doing something useful and generous. Jesus gently says she was anxious about many things when one thing was needed.
application.question: What useful task keeps pulling you away from simply sitting with Jesus?

context.heading: Bread for the coming day
context.body: The word for "daily" in the Lord's Prayer, epiousios, is almost unknown outside this prayer. Scholars suggest "needed for today," "necessary for existence" or "for the coming day." Each option points to the same posture: asking God for provision one day at a time, as Israel gathered manna.

context.heading: The finger of God
context.body: Jesus says He drives out demons by the daktylos ("finger") of God. Pharaoh's magicians used the same phrase when they could not copy the plague of gnats (Exodus 8:19). Jesus' exorcisms are an exodus-style display of God's power, and they mean the kingdom has arrived.

context.heading: Graves you walk over
context.body: Touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), so Jews whitewashed tombs to warn passersby. Jesus says the Pharisees are like adēlos ("unmarked") graves: people come into contact with their corruption without even knowing it. Matthew's version uses the opposite image of whitewashed tombs (Matthew 23:27).

theology.title: A Father who gives the Spirit
theology.body: If sinful fathers know how to give good gifts, "how much more" will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask (v. 13). Prayer is grounded not in wearing God down but in His generosity as Father. The greatest gift He gives is His own presence.

theology.title: Stronger than the strong man
theology.body: Jesus pictures Satan as a strong man guarding his house and Himself as the stronger one who overpowers him and takes his plunder (vv. 21–22). This echoes God's promise to take captives from the mighty (Isaiah 49:24–25). Jesus is also greater than Solomon and greater than Jonah (vv. 31–32): He is the wisdom and the message of God in person.

application.title: Asking for the best gift
application.body: Jesus ends His teaching on prayer by pointing to the Holy Spirit as the Father's gift. Most of our prayers are about circumstances.
application.question: What would change if you asked God for more of His Spirit as often as you ask Him to change your situation?

application.title: The swept but empty house
application.body: An evil spirit leaves, finds the house swept and in order but empty, and returns with seven worse (vv. 24–26). Removing bad habits is not the same as being filled with something better.
application.question: What have you cut out of your life without letting Jesus fill the space it left?

application.title: Clean cups, dirty insides
application.body: Jesus says the Pharisees clean the outside of the cup while the inside is full of greed. He calls them to give from the inside out.
application.question: What do you keep polished for others to see while the inside goes unattended?

context.heading: A fool with a loan called in
context.body: God calls the rich farmer aphrōn, "fool." In Scripture a fool is not unintelligent but lives as if God does not matter (Psalm 14:1). "Your soul is demanded of you" uses apaiteō, a word for calling in a loan. His life was never his own; it was on loan, and the lender wanted it back that night.

context.heading: Hanging in suspense
context.body: Jesus says not to be meteōrizomai, the root of our word "meteor." It means to be lifted up and left hanging, and was used of ships tossed on rough seas. Anxiety is pictured as being suspended in midair, unsettled and unable to find footing.

context.heading: Waiting for a late master
context.body: Wedding feasts could run for days, so servants could not know when their master would return. The second or third watch meant the dead of night. Then Jesus adds a shock: the returning master dresses to serve, seats his servants at the table and waits on them himself (v. 37).

theology.title: The owner of every life
theology.body: God is the giver and owner of life, to whom every person will give an account. "Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required" (v. 48). Judgment in this chapter is real but measured: God weighs what each person knew and was given. That is both a warning and a comfort.

theology.title: A baptism of fire and division
theology.body: Jesus says He has a baptism to undergo and is distressed until it is completed (v. 50), meaning His coming death. He brings division, even within families (vv. 51–53), echoing Micah 7:6. The peace He brings is real, but it comes through allegiance to Him, and that allegiance will cost some relationships.

application.title: A conversation with yourself
application.body: The rich farmer talks only to himself: "I will say to my soul" (v. 19). Saving was not his sin; leaving God and neighbor out of the plan was.
application.question: Who besides yourself has a real voice in your financial plans?

application.title: Follow the money
application.body: "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (v. 34). Money does not just reveal the heart; it also leads it.
application.question: If someone read only your bank statement, where would they say your heart is?

application.title: Fear the right one
application.body: Jesus tells His "friends" not to fear those who can only kill the body (vv. 4–5). Fear of people shrinks when we take God seriously.
application.question: Whose disapproval shapes your daily choices more than God's does?

context.heading: Two disasters in the headlines
context.body: No other ancient source records Pilate mixing Galileans' blood with their sacrifices or the collapse of the tower (pyrgos) of Siloam, but both fit what we know. The historian Josephus describes Pilate's violent clashes with Jewish crowds, and Siloam was a pool area in southern Jerusalem. One event was human cruelty and the other an accident; Jesus draws the same lesson from both.

context.heading: Untied like an ox
context.body: Jesus answers the synagogue ruler with a wordplay. Every farmer will luō ("untie") his ox or donkey on the Sabbath to water it (v. 15). Should not this daughter of Abraham, bound by Satan for eighteen years, be luō from her bond on the Sabbath? The day that celebrated rest and release was exactly the right day.

context.heading: Calling Herod a fox
context.body: Jesus calls Herod Antipas an alōpēx ("fox"). In Jewish usage a fox could suggest cunning, but also a minor, destructive creature compared with a lion. Antipas was not even a full king; Rome gave him the lesser title tetrarch. Jesus will not let this small ruler set His schedule.

theology.title: Patience that has a limit
theology.body: The vineyard owner looks for fruit for three years, and the gardener asks for one more (vv. 6–9). The prophets used vines and fig trees for Israel (Isaiah 5:1–7; Micah 7:1). God's patience is real: He delays judgment so people can repent (2 Peter 3:9). But the parable ends with an open question, and patience is not the same as indifference.

theology.title: Wings over Jerusalem
theology.body: Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings (v. 34). Scripture uses this picture for God Himself sheltering His people (Deuteronomy 32:11; Psalm 91:4; Ruth 2:12). Jesus speaks with God's own longing over the city, and His grief is real even as people come from east and west to the feast while many insiders are shut out (v. 29).

application.title: Tragedy is not a scorecard
application.body: When disaster strikes others, we instinctively wonder what they did to deserve it. Jesus turns the question back on His listeners: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
application.question: When something terrible happens to someone else, what conclusions do you quietly draw about them?

application.title: One more year
application.body: The gardener promises to dig and fertilize the barren tree for a year. Fruit does not appear by accident; it comes from tending.
application.question: If God gave you exactly one more year, what fruit would you want visible at the end of it?

application.title: When rules block rejoicing
application.body: A woman stands up straight for the first time in eighteen years, and the synagogue ruler's first response is irritation about timing. He had a rule ready before he had any joy.
application.question: Where do your ideas about how things should be done keep you from celebrating when someone is helped?

context.heading: Watched with suspicion
context.body: The guests are paratēreō, "watching closely," Jesus. The word suggests surveillance with hostile intent, the way one watches for a mistake. Luke uses it earlier when scribes and Pharisees watch to see if Jesus will heal on the Sabbath so they can accuse Him (6:7). Jesus heals anyway, then turns the scrutiny back on His observers.

context.heading: The second invitation
context.body: Wealthy hosts often sent invitations in advance, then a servant announced when the meal was ready. Accepting the first call and refusing the second was a public insult. The excuses are thin: no one buys a field unseen or oxen untested, and a new marriage did not cancel a prior commitment.

context.heading: Hate as a word of priority
context.body: Jesus says a disciple must miseō ("hate") father, mother, spouse and children. In Hebrew idiom, "hate" can mean to choose one over another: Leah was "hated" in the sense of loved less (Genesis 29:30–31). Matthew's parallel says, "Whoever loves father or mother more than Me" (Matthew 10:37). Jesus demands first place, not hostility.

theology.title: The banquet of God
theology.body: Isaiah foresaw the LORD preparing a rich feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6–8). Jesus tells hosts to invite "the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind" (v. 13), and the master in the parable sends for exactly that list (v. 21). God's house will be full, and it fills with people who know they cannot repay. "Compel them to come in" (v. 23) describes urgent invitation, not force.

theology.title: The God who lifts the lowly
theology.body: Jesus' seating advice echoes Proverbs 25:6–7, and His rule that the humble will be exalted runs through Scripture, from Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:7–8) to Mary's (Luke 1:52). God sees the person at the bottom of the table. He gives honor; it cannot be grabbed.

application.title: Your inner seating chart
application.body: Guests jostled for the best couches because seating showed rank. We do the same with titles, follower counts and who gets the first word in a meeting.
application.question: In which rooms do you find yourself quietly calculating your place?

application.title: A guest list with no return
application.body: Jesus tells His host to invite people who cannot invite him back. Generosity that expects reciprocity is just trade.
application.question: When did you last host someone who could never repay you in any way?

application.title: Salt that tastes of nothing
application.body: Jesus warns that salt can lose its saltiness and become useless (vv. 34–35). A faith that never costs anything can quietly become bland.
application.question: What part of your faith has gone flat because it has never cost you anything?

context.heading: Grumbling like the wilderness
context.body: The Pharisees and scribes diagongyzō, "kept muttering" among themselves. The same word family describes Israel grumbling against God in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8). Without noticing, the religious leaders cast themselves as the grumblers in Israel's story, complaining about God's provision for undeserving people.

context.heading: Living past saving
context.body: The younger son squanders his share living asōtōs, "recklessly." The word is built from a negative and the verb "to save," suggesting a life that cannot hold onto anything. Notice that the older brother later adds the detail about prostitutes (v. 30); the narrator never says it.

context.heading: Robe, ring and sandals
context.body: The father calls for the best stolē ("robe"), likely his own, to honor the son publicly. A ring may signal family authority, and sandals marked a son rather than a barefoot servant. Before the village could shame the boy, the father clothes him in status he did not earn.

theology.title: The God who comes looking
theology.body: In all three stories the owner searches: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine, the woman lights a lamp and sweeps. This is God's character from the start (Genesis 3:9) and His promise in Ezekiel 34:11–16: "I Myself will search for My sheep." Jesus eating with sinners is not a lapse in holiness; it is God on the search.

theology.title: Grace that offends the dutiful
theology.body: The father runs before his son finishes his rehearsed speech, and calls him "dead and alive again" (v. 24). Grace is given, not negotiated. Then the father goes out to the older brother too, pleading with him (v. 28). The story ends without telling us whether he goes in, because the question is aimed at every listener who has served for years and resents the party.

application.title: Coming to your senses
application.body: The son "came to himself" (v. 17) in a pigpen, starving. Sometimes it takes hitting bottom to see clearly what home always offered.
application.question: What would coming to your senses look like in the part of your life you keep avoiding?

application.title: The older brother's ledger
application.body: "All these years I've been slaving for you" (v. 29). The older son stayed home but thought of himself as a servant earning wages, not a son sharing everything.
application.question: Where do you resent God's kindness to someone you think deserves it less than you?

application.title: Still searching
application.body: The woman sweeps the whole house for one coin because it matters to her. The shepherd counts and notices one missing.
application.question: Who has drifted out of your church or friendships that you have stopped looking for?

context.heading: A manager's discount
context.body: A steward ran his master's estate and could make binding deals. A hundred batos ("baths") of olive oil was roughly 800 to 900 gallons, so halving the bill was a large favor. Some scholars think he cut out his own commission or hidden interest; others think he simply cheated. Either way, he used his master's money to secure his future, and Jesus commends his foresight, not his ethics.

context.heading: Tents that last forever
context.body: Jesus says faithful use of money gains friends who will welcome you into "eternal dwellings" (skēnē, literally "tents"). Tents were the most temporary homes there were, so the phrase is a deliberate paradox. It recalls the tabernacle, God's tent among His people. The permanent home is the one God gives.

context.heading: Hades and Abraham's side
context.body: Hadēs is the Greek name for the realm of the dead, used to translate Hebrew Sheol. Some Jewish writings of the time pictured the dead in separate places awaiting judgment. "Abraham's side" (kolpos, v. 22) suggests a place of honor at a banquet, reclining next to the host. As the Setting notes, Christians differ on how literally to read these details.

theology.title: Moses and the Prophets are enough
theology.body: The rich man wants Lazarus to warn his brothers. Abraham answers that they have Moses and the Prophets, and if they will not listen to Scripture, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead (vv. 29–31). Luke's readers know that Someone did rise. God has spoken clearly in His word, and the problem is not lack of evidence but unwillingness to hear.

theology.title: The God who knows hearts
theology.body: "God knows your hearts. What is highly valued among men is detestable before God" (v. 15). God's measure differs from society's. Jesus affirms that the law stands (v. 17) and then applies it sharply to marriage (v. 18); Christians differ on how this saying relates to the exceptions in Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:15.

application.title: Faithful when it's small
application.body: "Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much" (v. 10). Character shows up in expense reports, borrowed tools and small change.
application.question: How do you handle small amounts of money, time or trust when nobody is checking?

application.title: The man at your gate
application.body: The rich man knew Lazarus's name; he even asked for him later. Lazarus was close enough to see every day and easy enough to ignore.
application.question: Who is close enough for you to know by name but easy for you to step past?

application.title: Sneering at the hard sayings
application.body: The Pharisees, who loved money, ridiculed Jesus' teaching (v. 14). Mockery is often a defense when a teaching hits too close.
application.question: Which teaching of Jesus about money do you most want to explain away?

context.heading: Seven times in a day
context.body: Jesus says to forgive a brother who sins against you heptakis ("seven times") in a day and repents each time. Later rabbinic tradition taught forgiving a repeated offense up to three times. Seven, the number of completeness, means without counting. Forgiveness is paired with honest rebuke (v. 3), not with pretending nothing happened.

context.heading: Servants owed nothing extra
context.body: After a day of plowing, a servant still prepares his master's dinner. Disciples who obey should say, "We are achreios servants." The word is often translated "unworthy" or "worthless," but the sense is servants who have earned no special credit. They have only done their duty.

context.heading: The foreigner's word
context.body: Jesus calls the returning Samaritan an allogenēs, "foreigner." The same word appeared on warning inscriptions at the temple forbidding foreigners from entering its inner courts on pain of death, and examples have been found. The outsider who was barred from the temple is the one who returns to give glory to God at Jesus' feet.

theology.title: A great God, not great faith
theology.body: The apostles ask for more faith, and Jesus says faith the size of a mustard seed could uproot a tree (vv. 5–6). The power is not in the size of the faith but in the God it trusts. Then He adds the servant parable, so that no one turns faith into a performance that earns God's favor.

theology.title: Sudden as Noah's flood
theology.body: Jesus compares His coming to the days of Noah and Lot, when people were eating, marrying and building until judgment came (Genesis 6–7; 19). God's judgment interrupts ordinary life without warning. Christians read "one taken, one left" (vv. 34–35) differently, some as being taken in judgment and some as being gathered to the Lord. The shared point is readiness.

application.title: The thank-you you never sent
application.body: Ten were healed; one came back. The other nine were doing exactly what Jesus told them, yet missed the most important response.
application.question: What has God done for you this year that you never went back to thank Him for?

application.title: Duty without applause
application.body: Jesus' servant parable punctures our quiet expectation of credit for doing what we should. Obedience is not a favor to God.
application.question: Where are you secretly waiting for recognition for something you were simply supposed to do?

application.title: Remember Lot's wife
application.body: Lot's wife escaped Sodom but turned back to look (v. 32; Genesis 19:26). Her heart was still in the city she was leaving.
application.question: What part of your old life do you keep glancing back at?

context.heading: Refusing to lose heart
context.body: Luke says Jesus told this parable so they would pray and not enkakeō, "lose heart" or "give up." Paul uses the same word: "we do not lose heart" (2 Corinthians 4:16) and "let us not grow weary in doing good" (Galatians 6:9). Persistent prayer is the opposite of quiet resignation.

context.heading: A judge afraid of a black eye
context.body: The judge gives in so the widow will not hypōpiazō him. The word is a boxing term meaning to hit under the eye, and Paul uses it of disciplining his body (1 Corinthians 9:27). Here it may mean "wear me out" or "give me a public black eye" by shaming him. The humor is intentional: the powerful judge is cornered by a powerless widow.

context.heading: A camel and a needle
context.body: Jesus pictures the kamēlos ("camel"), the largest animal in the region, squeezing through a needle's eye. It is deliberate exaggeration for something humanly impossible. The popular idea of a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle's Eye has no ancient evidence behind it and softens the point Jesus is making.

theology.title: A God who is not like the judge
theology.body: Jesus argues from lesser to greater: if an unjust judge eventually helps, how much more will God bring justice for His chosen ones who cry to Him (v. 7). God is not reluctant or bribable. The real question Jesus raises is not God's faithfulness but ours: "Will He find faith on the earth?" (v. 8).

theology.title: Possible only with God
theology.body: The disciples ask, "Then who can be saved?" Jesus answers, "What is impossible with man is possible with God" (vv. 26–27). Salvation is God's work from start to finish. The tax collector goes home justified by asking for mercy, the children receive the kingdom without credentials, and a blind beggar who calls Jesus "Son of David" receives sight as Isaiah promised (Isaiah 35:5).

application.title: The prayer you stopped praying
application.body: The widow kept coming back. Many of us quit asking long before we would admit we have given up.
application.question: What prayer have you quietly stopped praying because the answer took too long?

application.title: Prayer by comparison
application.body: The Pharisee thanks God he is not like other people, especially "this tax collector." His prayer needed someone worse to stand next to.
application.question: Whom do you compare yourself to so that you can feel all right before God?

application.title: The one thing you lack
application.body: The ruler had kept the commandments, but Jesus named the one thing he could not let go of. The man left very sad.
application.question: If Jesus named the one thing you would struggle most to give up, what would it be?

context.heading: Paying back four times over
context.body: Zacchaeus admits he has sykophanteō, "extorted by false charges," a common tax-collector abuse. The law required returning what was taken plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7). Fourfold was the penalty for stealing and killing a sheep (Exodus 22:1). Zacchaeus volunteers the harshest standard and adds half his goods to the poor.

context.heading: A king the people did not want
context.body: Jesus tells of a nobleman who travels to a distant country to receive a kingdom, while a presbeia ("delegation") follows to oppose him. Many scholars think listeners would recall Archelaus, Herod's son, who went to Rome in 4 BC to have his rule confirmed while a Jewish delegation protested against him. Jesus was near Jericho, where Archelaus had built a palace.

context.heading: The day God came to visit
context.body: Jesus weeps that Jerusalem did not recognize the time of its episkopē, "visitation." In the Old Testament God "visits" His people to rescue or to judge (Genesis 50:24; Exodus 3:16). Zechariah sang that God had visited His people (1:68). The visit came, and the city missed it.

theology.title: The King on a borrowed colt
theology.body: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a colt, acting out Zechariah 9:9, where Zion's king comes humble and riding on a donkey. The crowd quotes Psalm 118:26 and adds "peace in heaven and glory in the highest" (v. 38), echoing the angels at His birth (2:14). If they were silent, Jesus says, the stones would cry out: creation itself knows its King.

theology.title: A house of prayer reclaimed
theology.body: Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7, "My house will be a house of prayer," and Jeremiah 7:11, "a den of robbers." Isaiah's line continues "for all nations," and the trading may have filled the court where Gentiles could pray. Malachi said the Lord would suddenly come to His temple to purify it (Malachi 3:1–3). Jesus acts as the temple's rightful Lord.

application.title: Restitution, not just regret
application.body: Zacchaeus did not stop at feeling sorry; he named specific debts and repaid them with interest. Real repentance often has a dollar amount attached.
application.question: Is there someone you have wronged where an apology is not enough and you owe them something concrete?

application.title: Wrapped in a cloth
application.body: The servant who hid his mina did it because he was afraid (v. 21). Fear of failure produced nothing at all.
application.question: What has God put in your hands that you have wrapped up and hidden out of fear?

application.title: Missing what is in front of you
application.body: Jerusalem did not know "the things that make for peace" even on the day they rode in on a donkey. Busy, religious people can miss God's visit entirely.
application.question: What might God be doing around you right now that you are too preoccupied to notice?

context.heading: Spies with sincere faces
context.body: The leaders send enkathetos, "spies," people planted in a crowd under false pretenses, who pretend to be sincere. Their goal is to catch Jesus in a statement that would let them hand Him over to the governor. The tax question was designed so that either answer would cost Him: support Rome and lose the people, or reject the tax and face Rome.

context.heading: Whose image is this?
context.body: A denarius of Tiberius bore his eikōn ("image") and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus. Many Jews found such coins offensive. Jesus' answer is sharper than it first sounds: the coin bears Caesar's image, but every human being bears God's image (Genesis 1:27). Give Caesar his coin and give God yourself.

context.heading: The stone at the head of the corner
context.body: Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22: the rejected stone has become kephalē ("head") of the corner, the key stone that anchors or completes a building. He adds that this stone will crush whoever it falls on (v. 18), echoing the stone that shatters earthly kingdoms in Daniel 2:34–35. The builders' rejection cannot stop God's construction.

theology.title: The beloved son sent last
theology.body: The vineyard story draws on Isaiah 5:1–7, where Israel is God's vineyard. The owner sends servant after servant, as God sent prophet after prophet, and finally "my beloved son" (v. 13), the same words the Father spoke at Jesus' baptism (3:22). Jesus tells His own death in advance. God's patience is long, but rejecting His Son brings judgment.

theology.title: David's Son and David's Lord
theology.body: Jesus asks how the Messiah can be David's son when David calls him "my Lord" in Psalm 110:1 (vv. 41–44). In that culture a father did not call his descendant lord. The answer the Gospels give is that the Messiah is both David's descendant by human birth and David's Lord by divine identity.

application.title: Stamped with God's image
application.body: If a coin belongs to the one whose image it carries, then you belong to God. That claim reaches past Sunday into your calendar, your body and your bank account.
application.question: What part of yourself are you still holding back from the God whose image you bear?

application.title: Questions as traps
application.body: The leaders asked about authority, taxes and resurrection, but none of them wanted an answer. They wanted a way to avoid submitting.
application.question: When you bring hard questions to God, do you want the answer or an exit?

application.title: Spiritual reputation
application.body: The scribes loved long robes, respectful greetings and the best seats, while devouring widows' houses (vv. 46–47). Religious status can become a costume.
application.question: What do you enjoy about being seen as a spiritual person?

context.heading: Two of the smallest coins
context.body: The widow gives two lepton, the smallest copper coins in circulation, each worth about one-128th of a denarius, a day's wage. She could have kept one. Jesus measures the gift not by its size but by what was left after giving: she gave all she had to live on.

context.heading: A temple dressed in gifts
context.body: People admire the temple adorned with beautiful stones and anathēma, "votive offerings" given to God. Herod's temple was famous for its massive white stones and gifts like a golden vine over the entrance described by Josephus. Within about forty years, in AD 70, Roman armies under Titus burned it.

context.heading: A heart weighed down
context.body: Jesus warns that hearts can be weighed down by kraipalē, the heavy, dull feeling after a night of drinking, along with drunkenness and the worries of life. He puts indulgence and anxiety side by side. Both leave a person sluggish and unready.

theology.title: The times of the Gentiles
theology.body: Jesus says Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles "until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (v. 24). Christians read this differently. Some see it as the whole gospel age; many also connect it with Paul's hope of a future turning of Israel to the Messiah (Romans 11:25–26). All agree that history runs on God's timetable, not Rome's.

theology.title: Words more lasting than the universe
theology.body: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away" (v. 33). Isaiah said the same of God's word (Isaiah 40:8; 51:6). Jesus claims for His own words the permanence that belongs to God's word. Everything else in this chapter can shake, but His promises cannot.

application.title: Giving that costs something
application.body: The rich gave out of their surplus; the widow gave out of her poverty. Jesus noticed the difference.
application.question: When did your giving last cost you something you actually noticed?

application.title: No need to rehearse
application.body: Jesus tells disciples facing trial not to prepare their defense in advance, because He will give them words and wisdom (vv. 14–15). Many of us rehearse arguments in our heads for hours.
application.question: What conversation are you rehearsing in your head instead of trusting God with it?

application.title: Dulled by comfort or worry
application.body: Jesus names both indulgence and anxiety as ways hearts get weighed down. One numbs us with pleasure, the other with fear.
application.question: Which dulls your spiritual attention more right now, comfort or worry?

context.heading: A new covenant in blood
context.body: Jesus calls the cup "the new diathēkē ("covenant") in My blood." At Sinai Moses sprinkled "the blood of the covenant" on the people (Exodus 24:8), and Jeremiah promised a new covenant with forgiven sins and God's law written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The Passover meal included several cups of wine, which is probably why Luke mentions two (vv. 17, 20).

context.heading: Rulers who call themselves benefactors
context.body: Kings who lord it over people are called euergetēs, "Benefactors." This was a real official title: Hellenistic kings and Roman patrons put it on coins and inscriptions, and Ptolemy III of Egypt was known as Euergetes. Jesus exposes the gap between the title and the domination behind it.

context.heading: Sifted like wheat
context.body: Satan asked to siniazō, "sift," the disciples like wheat, shaking them in a sieve. In Greek the first "you" is plural, meaning all of them, but in v. 32 Jesus says "I have prayed for you" in the singular, to Peter. The scene recalls Satan asking permission to test Job (Job 1–2).

theology.title: Numbered with the transgressors
theology.body: Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12, "He was numbered with the transgressors," and says it must be fulfilled in Him (v. 37). He explicitly identifies Himself with Isaiah's suffering servant, who bears the sin of many. The cross is not an accident; it is the plan God announced centuries before.

theology.title: The cup the Son accepts
theology.body: In the Prophets the "cup" often stands for God's wrath against sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus asks the Father to remove it, then prays, "Not My will, but Yours be done" (v. 42). His real human will submits to the Father's. The Son drinks the cup so that His people can drink the cup of the new covenant instead.

application.title: Competing at the table
application.body: Moments after the Last Supper, the disciples argue about who is greatest. Jesus answers that He is among them as one who serves.
application.question: Where are you competing for recognition in a place that was meant for service?

application.title: Prayed for before the fall
application.body: Jesus prayed for Peter before the denial and told him, "When you have turned back, strengthen your brothers" (v. 32). Peter's failure was going to become part of his ministry.
application.question: How could your worst failure become the thing you use to strengthen someone else?

application.title: Following at a distance
application.body: Peter followed Jesus, but "at a distance" (v. 54), close enough to watch and far enough to deny. Then a servant girl's question undid him.
application.question: In what setting do you keep enough distance from Jesus that no one would connect you to Him?

context.heading: A king hoping for a show
context.body: Herod Antipas had long wanted to see Jesus perform a sēmeion ("sign"), like a performer at court. This is the ruler who beheaded John the Baptist. Jesus gives him no miracle and no answer. Only Luke records that Herod and Pilate became friends that day (v. 12), united in rejecting Jesus.

context.heading: Green wood and dry
context.body: To the weeping women Jesus quotes what was probably a proverb: if they do this when the wood is hygros ("green, moist"), what will happen when it is dry? Green wood does not burn easily. Many scholars think He means that if Rome treats an innocent man this way, the judgment coming on guilty Jerusalem will be far worse.

context.heading: The curtain torn in two
context.body: The katapetasma ("curtain") most likely means the inner veil before the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest entered once a year. Its tearing signals that access to God is opened through Jesus' death (Hebrews 10:19–20). Luke places it in the darkness just before Jesus' final cry.

theology.title: The Righteous One condemned
theology.body: Luke repeats Jesus' innocence again and again: Pilate says it three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod finds nothing, a criminal says He has done nothing wrong (v. 41), and the centurion calls Him righteous (v. 47). Isaiah's servant is "the righteous one" who bears the iniquities of many (Isaiah 53:11). Meanwhile Barabbas, guilty of murder, walks free (v. 25). The innocent dies in place of the guilty.

theology.title: Into Your hands
theology.body: Jesus' last words in Luke come from Psalm 31:5: "Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit." Jewish tradition used this psalm as an evening prayer, and Jesus adds the word "Father." Even in death the Son trusts His Father completely. His prayer for His executioners' forgiveness (v. 34) shows the same heart.

application.title: The loudest voices
application.body: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent but gave in when the crowd's shouts prevailed (v. 23). He tried to wash his hands of a decision that was his to make.
application.question: Where are you letting the loudest voices push you toward a decision you know is wrong?

application.title: Not too far gone
application.body: A dying criminal with no time to make amends simply asks Jesus to remember him. He receives a promise for that very day.
application.question: Whom have you quietly written off as too far gone for grace?

application.title: Courage when it's too late to help
application.body: Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not agreed with their decision, publicly asks for Jesus' body (vv. 50–52). He stepped forward when following Jesus looked like a lost cause.
application.question: What would it cost you to identify publicly with Jesus when it is least convenient?

context.heading: Nonsense from the women
context.body: The apostles think the women's report is lēros, "nonsense" or "idle talk." Greek medical writers used the word for the babbling of a delirious patient. A woman's testimony carried less weight in many courts of the time, so a made-up story would hardly name women as the first witnesses. Luke names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Mary the mother of James.

context.heading: It was necessary
context.body: "Was it not necessary (dei) for the Christ to suffer these things and to enter His glory?" Dei expresses divine necessity, and Luke uses it at key points: Jesus "must" suffer (9:22; 17:25), Scripture "must" be fulfilled (22:37; 24:44). The cross was not a detour from God's plan but the road to glory.

context.heading: Clothed with power
context.body: Jesus tells the disciples to wait until they are enduō, "clothed," with power from on high. In the Greek Old Testament the Spirit of the LORD "clothed" Gideon (Judges 6:34). The promise points to Pentecost (Acts 1:8; 2:1–4), when the Spirit comes on the waiting church.

theology.title: A risen body that eats
theology.body: Jesus invites the disciples to touch Him and eats broiled fish in front of them (vv. 39–43). He is not a ghost or a vision but bodily raised, the same Jesus with real flesh and bones, now glorified. His resurrection is the firstfruits of the resurrection God promises His people (1 Corinthians 15:20). This is the faith of the Creed: on the third day He rose again.

theology.title: From Jerusalem to the nations
theology.body: Jesus says the Scriptures foretold His death, His resurrection and repentance for forgiveness proclaimed to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (vv. 46–47). God's promise to bless all nations through Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and to make His servant a light to the nations (Isaiah 49:6) now moves into motion. Jesus ascends with hands raised in blessing like a priest (Leviticus 9:22), and Acts continues the story.

application.title: Unrecognized on the road
application.body: The two disciples walked seven miles talking about Jesus without realizing He was beside them. Disappointment can blind us to His presence.
application.question: Where might Jesus be walking with you in a disappointment you have not yet recognized Him in?

application.title: Reading for Jesus
application.body: Jesus showed them Himself in Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms (v. 44). Much of the Old Testament reads differently when you know whose story it is.
application.question: Which part of the Old Testament have you never read looking for Jesus in it?

application.title: Joy that sends you back
application.body: The disciples returned to Jerusalem, the city where Jesus was killed, with great joy and continual worship (vv. 52–53). Meeting the risen Jesus sent them back into the hardest place, not away from it.
application.question: Where is the risen Jesus sending you back to with joy instead of dread?
